title: Variables, Data Types & Operators
description: Learn how Python stores data, the core types you'll use everywhere, and how to combine values with operators

lessons.title: Variables and Assignment
lessons.description: Store and label data with variables

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Create variables, understand naming rules, and reassign values.

sections.title: 📦 Creating Variables
sections.content:
A variable is a name that points to a value. Python figures out the type automatically — you don't declare it.

```python
x = 5
name = "Alice"
price = 9.99
is_active = True
```

**Naming Rules:**
• Must start with a letter or underscore
• Can contain letters, numbers, underscores
• Case-sensitive (`age` and `Age` are different)
• Cannot use reserved words like `for`, `if`, `class`

**Convention:** use `snake_case` for variable names, e.g. `total_price`.

sections.title: 🔁 Reassigning & Multiple Assignment
sections.content:
Variables can change value — and even type — at any time.

```python
x = 5
x = "now a string"  # totally legal

# Assign several at once
a, b, c = 1, 2, 3

# Same value to multiple names
x = y = z = 0
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Using a reserved keyword as a variable name, or forgetting Python is case-sensitive (`Name` != `name`).

questions.question: Which is a valid Python variable name?
questions.explanation: Names can't start with a digit, contain hyphens, or be reserved keywords.

questions.question: What does `x = y = 5` do?
options: Assigns 5 to both x and y
questions.explanation: Chained assignment gives the same value to every name in the chain.

questions.question: Python variables are...
questions.explanation: The variable itself has no fixed type — the value it refers to does.

questions.question: `a, b = 1, 2` is called...
questions.explanation: Multiple assignment via tuple unpacking.

questions.question: Which naming style is conventional for variables?
questions.explanation: PEP 8 recommends snake_case for variables and functions.

questions.question: Is `age` the same variable as `Age`?
questions.explanation: Case sensitivity means these are two distinct names.

questions.question: What happens after `x = 5` then `x = 'hi'`?
options: x now refers to the string 'hi'
questions.explanation: Reassignment simply points the name at a new value of any type.

questions.question: Reserved words like `if` and `class`...
options: Cannot be used as variable names
Must be capitalized to be used
questions.explanation: Keywords are reserved by the language grammar.

lessons.title: Numbers and Type Conversion
lessons.description: Work with int, float, and convert between types

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Distinguish int/float, do arithmetic, and convert types with int()/float()/str().

sections.title: 🔢 Number Types
sections.content:
Python has two main numeric types you'll use constantly.

```python
age = 25          # int
price = 19.99      # float
complex_num = 2 + 3j  # complex (rare)
```

**Arithmetic Operators:**
```python
7 + 3   # 10  addition
7 - 3   # 4   subtraction
7 * 3   # 21  multiplication
7 / 3   # 2.333... true division (always float)
7 // 3  # 2   floor division
7 % 3   # 1   modulus (remainder)
7 ** 2  # 49  exponent
```

sections.title: 🔄 Type Conversion
sections.content:
Convert between types explicitly when you need to.

```python
int("42")     # 42
float("3.14") # 3.14
str(100)      # '100'
int(3.99)     # 3 (truncates, doesn't round)
round(3.99)   # 4
```

Mixing types in input often causes bugs — `input()` always returns a string, so convert it:

```python
age = int(input("Age: "))
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting `input()` returns a string, so `input("Age: ") + 1` raises a TypeError.

questions.question: What does `7 // 2` return?
questions.explanation: Floor division discards the remainder and returns an int here.

questions.question: What is `int("42")`?
questions.explanation: Converts the string to an integer.

questions.question: `input()` always returns a...
questions.explanation: You must convert it explicitly if you need a number.

questions.question: What is `10 % 3`?
questions.explanation: Modulus gives the remainder of division: 10 = 3*3 + 1.

questions.question: `int(3.99)` returns...
questions.explanation: int() truncates toward zero, it doesn't round.

questions.question: What type does `7 / 2` return?
questions.explanation: The `/` operator always produces a float, even for even division.

questions.question: `round(3.99)` returns...
questions.explanation: round() rounds to the nearest integer by default.

questions.question: What is `2 ** 10`?
questions.explanation: ** is exponentiation: 2 to the power of 10.

lessons.title: Booleans and None
lessons.description: Understand True/False logic and the absence of a value

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use bool values, understand truthy/falsy, and know when to use None.

sections.title: ✅ Booleans
sections.content:
`bool` has exactly two values: `True` and `False` (capitalized).

```python
is_valid = True
has_error = False

5 > 3   # True
5 == 5  # True
5 != 3  # True
```

**Truthy / Falsy values:** Many things behave like booleans in conditions.
```python
bool(0)      # False
bool("")     # False
bool([])     # False
bool(None)   # False
bool(1)      # True
bool("hi")   # True
```

sections.title: 🚫 None
sections.content:
`None` represents 'no value' — not zero, not empty, literally nothing assigned.

```python
result = None

if result is None:
    print("Nothing here yet")
```

Use `is None` / `is not None` rather than `== None` — it's the Pythonic convention.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing `if x == None` instead of `if x is None`, or confusing an empty string/list with None.

questions.question: How do you write Python's boolean values?
questions.explanation: Python booleans are capitalized: True and False.

questions.question: What is `bool("")`?
questions.explanation: An empty string is falsy.

questions.question: Preferred way to check for no value?
questions.explanation: `is None` is the Pythonic way to compare identity with None.

questions.question: What is `bool([])`?
questions.explanation: Empty containers are falsy.

questions.question: `None` represents...
questions.explanation: None is its own distinct type meaning 'nothing assigned'.

questions.question: What is `bool(1)`?
questions.explanation: Non-zero numbers are truthy.

questions.question: Which comparison returns a bool?
questions.explanation: Comparisons like > return True or False.

questions.question: What is `5 != 3`?
questions.explanation: != means 'not equal', and 5 is not equal to 3.

lessons.title: Operators
lessons.description: Arithmetic, comparison, logical, and assignment operators

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Combine comparison and logical operators to build conditions.

sections.title: ⚖️ Comparison Operators
sections.content:
Compare two values; result is always a bool.

```python
5 == 5   # True (equal)
5 != 3   # True (not equal)
5 > 3    # True
5 < 3    # False
5 >= 5   # True
5 <= 4   # False
```

sections.title: 🔗 Logical Operators
sections.content:
Combine boolean expressions.

```python
age = 25
has_id = True

age >= 18 and has_id   # True — both must be true
age < 18 or has_id     # True — at least one is true
not has_id             # False — flips the value
```

sections.title: ➕ Assignment Operators
sections.content:
Shortcuts for updating a variable in place.

```python
x = 10
x += 5   # x = x + 5  -> 15
x -= 3   # 12
x *= 2   # 24
x /= 4   # 6.0
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Confusing `=` (assignment) with `==` (comparison) — a very common beginner bug.

questions.question: What does `==` do?
questions.explanation: == checks whether two values are equal.

questions.question: `5 > 3 and 2 > 4` evaluates to...
questions.explanation: Both sides must be True for `and`; the second is False.

questions.question: What does `x += 5` mean?
questions.explanation: It's shorthand for reassigning x to x plus 5.

questions.question: `not True` is...
questions.explanation: not flips a boolean value.

questions.question: `5 != 5` is...
questions.explanation: 5 is equal to 5, so 'not equal' is False.

questions.question: `3 > 1 or 1 > 3` is...
questions.explanation: or only needs one side to be True.

questions.question: Which is a common beginner mistake?
options: Using = instead of == in a condition
questions.explanation: A single `=` assigns; conditions need `==` to compare.

questions.question: What does `x *= 2` do if x is 5?
questions.explanation: x becomes x * 2 = 10.

lessons.title: Input and Output
lessons.description: Get input from users and format output cleanly

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use input(), print() with options, and f-strings for formatting.

sections.title: ⌨️ Getting Input
sections.content:
`input()` pauses the program and waits for the user to type something, always returning a string.

```python
name = input("What's your name? ")
age = int(input("Age: "))  # convert if you need a number
```

sections.title: 🖨️ print() Options
sections.content:
print() has useful keyword arguments beyond just the message.

```python
print("Hello", "World")            # Hello World
print("a", "b", sep="-")           # a-b
print("Loading", end="...")        # no newline after
print("Done")
```

sections.title: ✨ f-strings
sections.content:
The cleanest way to build strings with variables inside them.

```python
name = "Ana"
score = 92.5
print(f"{name} scored {score:.1f}%")
# Ana scored 92.5%
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to convert `input()` to a number before doing math with it.

questions.question: What type does `input()` return?
questions.explanation: Always a string, regardless of what the user types.

questions.question: What does `print("a", "b", sep="-")` output?
questions.explanation: sep controls the separator between printed arguments.

questions.question: What does an f-string start with?
questions.explanation: f"..." marks a formatted string literal.

questions.question: `f"{score:.1f}"` formats score to...
questions.explanation: `.1f` means fixed-point with 1 digit after the decimal.

questions.question: What does `end="..."` do in print()?
options: Adds ... instead of a newline after output
questions.explanation: end replaces the default newline character.

questions.question: To read a number from input you should...
options: Wrap input() in int() or float()
questions.explanation: input() is always a string, so convert explicitly.

questions.question: Which correctly embeds a variable in an f-string?
questions.explanation: Curly braces embed expressions in an f-string.

questions.question: `print("x", "y")` by default separates with...
questions.explanation: The default sep value is a single space.
